name: Humanin
route: Injection in research and gray-market use
status: Not FDA-approved and not on FDA compounding lists; no human trials; WADA bans non-approved drugs like it
mechanism: A short peptide encoded in mitochondrial DNA that protects cells from stress-induced death and, in animals, improves insulin sensitivity

article.summary: Humanin is a short mitochondrial peptide first found in a screen for Alzheimer's protection. Evidence comes from cells and animals, no human trials exist, and it is not FDA-approved.
article.takeaway: Humanin is a peptide of about two dozen amino acids, encoded in mitochondrial DNA, that protected cultured nerve cells from Alzheimer's-related toxicity when it was discovered in 2001.[^1] In rodents, humanin and more potent analogs improved insulin action, and in aged mice it improved cognition.[^2][^3] In people, researchers have only measured natural levels and gene variants; the searches for this entry found no controlled trial of injected humanin. It is not FDA-approved, and WADA's ban on non-approved substances would apply to it.[^4]
glance: Not approved; no human efficacy trials
Injection in research and gray-market use; no approved dosing
Cell and rodent studies; human data are observational[^3]
Not named by WADA, but unapproved drugs are banned under S0[^4]

blocks.text: In 2001 researchers screening for genes that rescue nerve cells from toxicity tied to familial Alzheimer's disease found one that encodes a short secreted polypeptide, which they named Humanin.[^1] It is also made from the mitochondrial genome, and it belongs to a small family of mitochondrial-derived peptides.[^5] In cell and animal work it protects cells under stress and affects insulin signaling, partly through the hypothalamus in the brain.[^2]

items: **Cells:** humanin blocked the death of nerve cells exposed to Alzheimer's-related toxins[^1]
**Rodents:** infusions of humanin or potent analogs improved insulin sensitivity, and one analog lowered blood glucose in diabetic rats[^2]; in aged mice humanin improved cognition[^3]

**People:** a variant in the humanin-coding region of mitochondrial DNA lowers circulating humanin and was linked to faster cognitive aging in older adults, which suggests a role but does not show that injections help[^3]
**No human trial data:** safety, effective amounts and long-term effects of injected humanin are unknown
**Context-dependent effects:** a review reported that in senescent cells humanin and MOTS-c raised inflammatory signaling, so cell protection is not simply beneficial[^6]
**Open question:** because humanin blocks cell death, it is unknown whether it could also help damaged cells survive in people; this has not been studied
**Quality:** illegally sold peptide drugs have shown highly variable amounts, low purity and toxic metals such as arsenic and lead[^7]

blocks.text: Humanin is not an FDA-approved drug, and it does not appear on the FDA's May 2026 list of bulk substances nominated for pharmacy compounding.[^8] WADA does not name it, but its S0 class prohibits at all times any pharmacological substance with no approval for human therapeutic use, which would cover humanin.[^4]

Humanin is interesting mitochondrial biology with good animal data. No human trials of the peptide exist, so claims about longevity, brain protection or diabetes are speculation. It has no approved use, and athletes subject to testing should treat it as banned.

evidence.label: Preclinical: cell and animal studies only
evidence.text: The evidence is cell culture and rodent work, plus observational human genetics.[^1][^2][^3] No controlled human study of the peptide itself was found.

faq.a: That is a hypothesis. Natural levels and gene variants connect to cognitive aging in observational data, but there are no trials showing injections slow aging.[^3]

faq.q: How is humanin different from MOTS-c?
faq.a: Both are mitochondrial-derived peptides. [MOTS-c](/peptides/mots-c) acts mainly on muscle metabolism, while humanin was found as a neuroprotective factor.[^1]
It is sold online 'for research use only'. That label does not mean it is approved, tested for people or made to pharmaceutical standards.[^7]
